newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks still off at close, pact and rates.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks still off at close, pact and rates.

text.p: Mexican stocks closed lower Monday after a lackluster session in a market dulled by prospects of primary interest rate hikes and mixed reactions to the new national economic pact.

"The session was very listless. There's still uncertainty as they did not deal with issues like privatisation, and energy costs will go up by more than the inflation target," said Santos Herrera, analyst at the Estrategia Bursatil brokerage.
The blue chip IPC index closed down 16.81 points, or 0.52 percent, at 3,216.47. Volume was just 54.8 million shares traded, and even that mediocre figures was inflated by hefty cross trades.
The Alliance for Economic Growth was signed on Saturday, the latest in a series of economic pacts between government, business and labour leaders reached at regular intervals since 1987.

The pact provided for the minimum wage to rise by 17 percent in December, and for electricity and other energy costs to rise by up to 22 percent. Growth and inflation were forecast at 4 percent and 15 percent, respectively, for 1997.
"The market did not like the projected deficit figure, either," Herrera added. "What's more, they're expecting primary rates to increase tomorrow."
Traders added that the late slide by the Dow Jones also dragged Mexican stocks down.

The ADRs of telephone firm Telmex and media group Televisa closed down 1/4 and 5/8, respectively, at 30-5/8, and 26-1/2. Their L and CPO series shares closed down 10 centavos (1 cent) and 3 pesos (38 cents) down, respectively, at 12.18 pesos ($1.54) and 105.40 pesos ($13.33).
Financial stock GFInver headed the percentage leaders after having been hit very hard last week. The BCP series closed up five centavos (1 cent) at 70 centavos (9 cents).
On the broad market, losers outnumbered gainers by 51 to 23, out of a total of 93 stocks that changed hands.
A technical analyst said he did not expected trade in the Bolsa to pick up for about two weeks.

"The market is now waiting for official economic policy criteria for 1997 (due mid-November) to see if they underline earnings reports, which were good after the severe economic crisis last year," he said.
"The only stocks worth buying now are those which have good long-term fundamentals," he added.
